hero_lede: My app verifies that a Yape payment on a customer's screen is real.
hero_role3: Scope — Research → UX design → development → security → testing
hero_short: A queue at a market stall: a customer shows a screenshot saying the payment went through, and the merchant has seconds to accept. Every field on the confirmation can be faked except the operation number, and the app checks it, here against mock records rather than a live bank, before the goods leave. A secure keypad with randomized digits, double-click prevention and private-data protection guard the interface. Researched, designed and built in under a week, in a stack I had never used.
act0_scan1: Yape began as a way to send money to a phone number. Today much of Peru pays with it daily.
act0_scan2: It stopped being a transfer app long ago: credit, bill payments, a marketplace and remittances. A super app.
act0_scan3: Its success created a new fraud: if everyone trusts the confirmation screen, fake the screen.
act0_c1_x: Cash still matters in Peru, but its share fell sharply as e-payments took over daily commerce, led by Yape and other e-wallets.
act0_c2_x: A market stall or bodega: the customer shows a confirmation, the queue waits, and the merchant has seconds to decide.
act0_c3_x: The most exposed are small merchants and independent workers, for whom one fake payment can erase a day's earnings.
act1_c1_txt: A payment confirmation, on a phone, held up at your counter —
act1_c2_txt: an image, where every field is text that can be forged.
act1_bridge: The fake reproduces exactly what you are looking at. That is why staring harder fails.
act1_scan1: Peru's wallet boom outran its trust infrastructure, and the fake receipt is the hole it left.
act1_scan2: A security code shipped to close it. The public guidance still does not mention the code.
act1_rv_txt: I benchmarked three innovation-center banks in markets like Peru: Nubank, Nequi and Attijariwafa. All three treat verifiable payment trust as core product, so the gap is real. Merchant finance tools were a crowded space and onboarding drifts into regulated identity; payment trust won because it is urgent and solvable in front-end alone.
act1_receipt_alt: A Yape payment confirmation screen showing an amount in soles, a recipient name, a date and time, a three-digit security code, and an operation number.
act1_receipt_cap: The surface the fraud copies. Amount, recipient, date, security code — every line here is text on an image. Only the operation number is written by the bank's own record.
act2_scan: With the exact design system I could build or redesign the whole app, but that isn't the purpose. This case solves one real fraud problem with front-end alone, with every framework, security and code decision understood and backed by me.
act2_s1_x: I read the front-end requirements Peru's largest bank hires for, mapped them against my skills and aimed this project at the gap.
act2_s2_x: I left the vanilla web this site is built on and entered frameworks and app development, to test first-hand what I can build.
act2_s3_x: Reshaping a successful super app takes years. I chose to learn what solving one banking problem with front-end really takes.
sol_s1_alt: Market stall: the merchant's phone shows a green check mark and the shopping bag changes hands.
sol_s1_t: Know it is paid before handing the order
sol_s1_x: Trust & Verify confirms if the transfer occurred by checking the bank operation rather than a screenshot, protecting your store merchandise.
sol_s2_alt: The merchant's phone flags a mismatch beside the customer's screenshot.
sol_s2_t: See what does not match and say why
sol_s2_x: The app highlights the exact discrepancy against the customer's payment receipt, allowing you to explain calmly why the purchase cannot proceed.
sol_s3_alt: Busy checkout: a keypad with scrambled digits and a name protected behind dots.
sol_s3_t: Type securely in front of everyone
sol_s3_x: A randomized numeric keypad makes your keystrokes hard to follow, and customer names and phone numbers stay masked at every checkout.
act4_c1_t: React — one source of truth for every screen
act4_c1_x: React draws every screen from the app's data, never the reverse, so what the merchant sees always matches what the app knows. In a trust tool, that guarantee is the product.
act4_c1_rv_btn: Why React, and not vanilla or Angular
act4_c1_rv_txt: The one failure a verification tool can't survive is a stale screen showing "verified" for a cancelled check. In React the interface is a function of state, so a verdict can't tear under rapid updates. Vanilla would mean hand-wiring every listener, and this build's one real defect was a missed listener. Angular would work, but adds a large framework to a single-job build.
act4_c2_x: TypeScript is JavaScript with a strict proofreader: it catches whole classes of errors before the code runs. In a tool that tells a merchant to trust a payment, that net isn't optional.
act4_c2_rv_txt: Every receipt field, verdict state, and API response has a declared shape, so a malformed record cannot silently flow into a verdict. The compiler runs as a CI gate on every push — the same discipline production banking code expects: typed contracts, automated checks, continuous integration.
act4_c3_x: The security layer works like a film set: the heavy bank infrastructure is openly staged scenery, while every lock the merchant touches is real, working and tested.
act4_c3_rv_btn: What is scenery, what is the lock
act4_c3_rv_txt: The scenery shows the sector's security vocabulary (TLS 1.2, RSA-2048 key pairs, mutual certificate authentication, adaptive risk scoring) on fabricated material, badged SIMULATED throughout. The lock is what the merchant touches: an in-app keypad no third-party keyboard can read, shuffling digits, an execution lock, a blocking overlay and privacy masking.
act4_c4_x: Before trusting the build, I wrote a six-scenario test protocol from the case research: does it tell a fake from a real payment, and does it avoid misfiring under pressure?
act4_c4_rv_txt: 1: a forged amount on a real operation number is caught and named. 2: an unreadable security code never counts as a mismatch. 3: a double-tap or mid-flight cancel never fires the check twice. 4: the action stays inert until its preconditions hold. 5: the busy overlay truly blocks the page. 6: privacy masking never leaks a full name or number.
act4_synthesis: Only the operation number comes from the bank; the rest can be faked.

act5_hl1_x: Across six fraud scenarios. None waived.
act5_hl2_x: Typecheck, tests, build, drift and paths.
act5_hl3_x: First app build, first use of this stack.
act5_ins1: The fastest artifact in this portfolio is also its most technical. That inversion is the finding.
act5_ins2: What transfers. Any stack a client's problem requires is now within reach, with every decision owned and every claim checkable.
act5_fn1: Method. Figures counted from the repository and the recorded test run (Node 24.18.0, Vitest 3.2.7, TypeScript 5.9.3, 15 Jul 2026), verifiable at the linked source. Staged security demonstrations are described, and badged, in The Architecture above.
act5_fn2: Front-end only. No backend services, by constraint; 3 API endpoints consumed, with real request handling against mock fixtures.
act5_fn3: In the client. Security controls run in the browser, among them a secure keypad, shuffled digits, an execution lock, a blocking overlay and privacy masking.
act6_h1_x: I thought app development belonged to career developers. This build broke that ceiling: I now work the technical side while owning every strategic call, starting with the stack.
act6_h2_x: My fastest portfolio artifact yet, without typing a line of code and without vibe-coding shortcuts. Every framework, security and code decision was directed, reviewed and understood by me.
act6_h3_t: Knowing what each tool is for
act6_h3_x: Gemini compiled fifteen app screenshots into one master flow file. Claude Code ran deployment prompts I wrote as reusable skills, each run directed, reviewed and mine.
act6_h4_x: Banking is too wide to enter everywhere at once. A short study aimed at one real fraud mechanism, seen purely through front-end eyes, not as UX, redesign or innovation theatre.
independence: An independent case study. Not affiliated with, endorsed by, or connected to Yape or BCP. Built against fabricated fixtures. No real payment, account, or ledger is involved.
